questions.question: Match the following: 1. Simple squamous epithelium a) Proximal convoluted tubule 2. Simple cuboidal epithelium b) Gallbladder 3. Simple columnar epithelium c) Femoral Endothelium

explanation.text: Simple epithelia consist of a single layer of cells and are primarily found at interfaces where selective diffusion, absorption, and secretion occur. They are of three types. Types of Simple epithelium Description Simple squamous epithelium Pavemented epithelium Flattened, irregularly shaped cells forming a continuous surface.

Lining surfaces of gas and fluid exchange Lining pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal cavities to enable fluid exchange and reduce friction. Peritoneum (mesothelium) Vascular endothelium Simple cuboidal epithelium The cells are polygonal and nucleus is round located in the center of the cell.

Usually lines small ducts and tubules that have excretory, secretory or absorptive functions Collecting tubules of the kidney Small excretory ducts of the salivary glands and pancreas. Microvilli- PCT of kidney Simple columnar epithelium Tall columnar cells with the nuclei being located in the middle of the cells. Non-ciliated cells have secretory function whereas ciliated cells help in transport. Non-ciliated- Gallbladder lining.
Microvilli- Small intestine Surface cilia- Fallopian tube Pseudostratification- Respiratory tract Goblet cells- Small and large bowel Stereocilia- Vas deferens

questions.question: Given below are two histological images 1 and 2, which of the following pairs accurately represents the tissues depicted?

explanation.text: Trachea Urinary Bladder Epithelium: Lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, goblet cells, serous cells, and basal cells (neuroendocrine and stem cells). Ciliated columnar cells are more abundant in the lower trachea, while goblet and basal cells are more common in the upper trachea. Lamina Propria: Loose, highly vascular connective tissue beneath the epithelium, becoming more condensed at deeper levels with fibroelastic tissue.

Submucosa: Contains seromucinous glands that decrease in number toward the lower trachea; serous cells stain strongly, mucous cells stain poorly with H&E. Hyaline cartilage rings support the trachea, with the submucosa merging into the perichondrium or fibroelastic tissue between the rings. Epithelium: Lined with transitional epithelium, which forms many folds when the bladder is in a relaxed state.

The bladder wall consists of three smooth muscle layers – inner longitudinal, outer circular, and outermost longitudinal, known collectively as the detrusor muscle. These layers of smooth muscle and elastic fibers contract during micturition. Muscularis Mucosa: Separate the lamina propria from the submucosa, but it is often incomplete and not always visible. Adventitia: The outer adventitial coat contains arteries, veins, and lymphatic vessels.

Stomach (Option A & C): The stomach is lined by simple columnar epithelium with gastric pits and glands, including surface mucous cells, mucous neck cells, parietal cells, and chief cells. It would not typically show the features of the urinary bladder or trachea. Fig. Histology of stomach Lymph node (Option A & C): A lymph node features a capsule, cortex with lymphatic follicles, and a medulla with medullary cords and sinuses.
It does not match the typical histological features of the trachea or urinary bladder. Fig. Histology of lymph node

questions.question: Which of the following structures is characterized by the presence of compound tubuloalveolar mucous glands in the submucosa, and a muscular layer that transitions from skeletal to smooth muscle?

explanation.text: The esophagus is lined with nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium and contains mucous glands (esophageal glands proper) in its submucosa for lubrication. Its muscular layer transitions from skeletal muscle (upper third) to smooth muscle (lower third), characteristic of the process of swallowing. Structure Description Esophagus Has four layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and adventitia.

Lumen lined with nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Submucosa - compound tubuloalveolar mucous glands, known as esophageal glands proper, which aid in lubrication. The upper third of the esophagus has predominantly skeletal muscle due to voluntary control during swallowing. In the middle third, there is a gradual transition to smooth muscle, and the lower third consists entirely of smooth muscle.
Lacks a serous covering, except for a short section near its lower end.

**Stomach (Option B ruled out):** The epithelium-forming glands are supported by Lamina Propria, a connective tissue. It has a peritoneum called serosa, which is missing from the oesophagus. Lined by Simple columnar epithelium and forms some gastric glands Mucosa contains gastric pits or gastric foveolae. The gastric glands contain: Surface mucous cells- Bicarbonate ions Mucous neck cells - mucus Parietal (Oxyntic) cells- HCL & Intrinsic Factor. Chief, peptic or zymogenic cells- Pepsin Neuroendocrine cells- Serotonin & Gastrin hormone. Small Intestine (Option C & D ruled out) Small intestine has columnar epithelium, which has villi, and microvilli leading to formation of brush border epithelium. The intestinal villi are lined by a simple columnar epithelium which is continuous with the crypts. Plicae circulares (Valves of Kerckring) are circular folds given by the mucosa and submucosa. Microvilli are finger-like projections to increase the surface area for absorption. Lymphoid clusters called Peyer’s patches are characteristically found in the lamina propria of the small intestine. Cells in the mucosa are: Enterocytes Paneth cells- defence Goblet cells- Mucin Neuroendocrine cells- hormones

questions.question: A 28-year-old patient with recurrent abdominal pain undergoes an endoscopic biopsy of the small intestine. The pathologist observes cells with prominent eosinophilic secretory granules located in the deeper parts of the intestinal crypts. These cells are known to produce substances that destroy bacteria. Which of the following cell types is the pathologist most likely observing as shown below?

explanation.text: The cells located in the deeper parts of the intestinal crypts having prominent eosinophilic secretory granules are Paneth cells, which produce lysozyme that destroys bacteria and other microorganisms in the small intestine.

Cells in Small Intestine Cell Type Location Function Characteristics Absorptive Columnar Cells (Enterocytes) (Option A) Luminal surface (villi) Absorption of amino acids, carbohydrates, and lipids - Oval nucleus in lower part - Striated border (microvilli) - Junctional complexes and desmosomes Goblet Cells Scattered among columnar cells, increasing in number towards ileum Mucus secretion - Expanded upper part with mucin granules - Flattened nucleus near base - Abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum Undifferentiated Cells Walls of intestinal crypts - Proliferate and migrate to villi - Differentiate into absorptive or goblet cells - Columnar cells Paneth Cells (Zymogen Cells) Deeper parts of intestinal crypts - Produce lysozyme (destroys bacteria) - May produce other enzymes - Prominent eosinophilic secretory granules - Considerable Golgi apparatus - Rough endoplasmic reticulum Endocrine Cells (Argentaffin/Enterochromaffin Cells) (Option D) Epithelial lining, most numerous near lower ends of crypts Secrete endocrine substances - Membrane-bound vesicles with neuroactive substances - Granules stain with silver salts M Cells (Option B) Overlying Peyer's patches - Engulf and transport microbes to basolateral surface - Stimulate gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) -Antigen-presenting function - Microfolds instead of microvilli

questions.question: Match the following: 1. Cervix a) 2. Fallopian tube b) 3. Ovary c) 4. Uterus d) 5. Vagina e)

explanation.text: Structures of the Female Reproductive Tract Ovary The ovary's cortex contains numerous follicles at different developmental stages, along with postovulatory structures like corpora lutea and degenerated follicles. The superficial cortex is fibrous, known as the tunica albuginea, and is covered by germinal epithelium, a continuation of the peritoneum. The highly vascular medulla supports the ovarian structure.

Fallopian Tube Mucosal lining with branching longitudinal folds, especially prominent in the ampulla, the usual site of fertilization. The wall consists of an inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer, while the serosa, continuous with the broad ligament, has a mesothelial surface. The epithelium is composed of ciliated, non-ciliated secretory, and intercalated cells.

Ciliated cells help propel the ovum with their wave-like motion, while non-ciliated cells secrete a fluid that nourishes and protects the ovum. The ratio of ciliated to non-ciliated cells varies with ovarian hormones, and intraepithelial lymphocytes are present. Uterus The uterus is a pear-shaped organ about 7 cm long, with a thick myometrium that provides support and expels the fetus during birth.

The endometrium, measuring 1 to 5 mm, varies in thickness throughout the menstrual cycle and supports fetal development. The endometrium has three distinct layers: the stratum basalis (deepest, stable layer), the stratum spongiosum (intermediate, spongy appearance), and the stratum compactum (superficial, compact layer).

The stratum functionalis, comprising the compact and spongy layers, undergoes significant changes and is shed during menstruation. Cervix The cervix consists of the endocervical canal lined by tall columnar mucus-secreting cells and the ectocervix lined by thic k stratified squamous epithelium, adapted to different environments.

The squamocolumnar junction between the ectocervix and endocervical epithelium is located at the external os and marks an abrupt transition. The cervical stroma is primarily composed of collagenous tissue with some smooth muscle and is infiltrated by leukocytes for defense against infection.

Hormonal changes during the menstrual cycle affect mucus secretion, with thinner mucus facilitating sperm passage around ovulation and thicker mucus forming a protective plug post-ovulation. Vagina The vaginal wall consists of a mucosal layer lined by stratified squamous epithelium, a sm ooth muscle layer, and an outer adventitial layer. The lamina propria is rich in elastin and small

veins but lacks glands. Lubrication comes from cervical mucus and secretions from the labia minora. The muscle layer has ill-defined inner circular and outer longitudinal arrangements, allowing for distension during childbirth. The epithelium undergoes cyclical changes in glycogen levels, which is metabolized by bacteria to produce lactic acid, inhibiting pathogenic growth.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the structure of sperm is true?

options.A: The head of sperm contains a central core of axoneme.
options.B: The principal piece of the tail contains hyaluronidase.
options.C: The neck of the sperm contains centrioles.
options.D: The tail contains the nucleus of the sperm.

explanation.text: The neck of the sperm contains centrioles, which play a crucial role in cell division and in forming the axoneme of the flagellum. Structure of Sperm Head Approximately 7 µm long with a flattened pear shape.

Nucleus: Contains very condensed chromatin with areas of dispersed chromatin known as nuclear vacuoles. (Option D) Acrosomal Cap: Surrounds the anterior two-thirds of the nucleus; a membrane-bound vesicle containing glycoproteins and hydrolytic enzymes (e.g., hyaluronidase) that assist in fertilization by dissolving the zona pellucida. (Option B) Neck This is a short segment linking the head to the tail.

Contain remnants of centrioles, one of which forms the axoneme of the flagellum. Often retains some cytoplasmic material in this region. Tail Divided into three parts: Middle piece, principal piece, and end piece. Middle Piece: Contains the flagellar axoneme surrounded by nine outer dense fibres and tightly packed elongated mitochondria arranged in a helix for energy.

Principal Piece: Constitutes most of the tail's length; has a central core with axoneme and coarse fibres, surrounded by fibrous ribs arranged circularly. Features dorsal and ventral columns for potential propulsion during movement. (Option A) End Piece: Short tapering portion containing only the axoneme.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the structure of the testis is FALSE?

options.A: The testis is surrounded by the tunica vaginalis.
options.C: The ductuli efferentes carry sperm from the epididymis to the rete testis.
options.D: The blood-testis barrier is formed by sertoli cells.

explanation.text: The ductuli efferentes carry sperm from the rete testis to the epididymis, not the other way around. Testis Anatomy Testis descends from the posterior peritoneal cavity wall to the scrotum during embryological

development. Tunica Vaginalis: Testis is surrounded by a double layer of mesothelium (visceral and parietal layers), enclosing a potential space filled with serous fluid for lubrication. (Option A) Tunica Albuginea: Capsule of the testis, forms incomplete collagenous septa dividing the testis into ~250 lobules.

Seminiferous Tubules: 1-4 convoluted tubes in each lobule, responsible for sperm production. (Option B) Rete Testis: Convergence point for seminiferous tubules. Ductuli Efferentes: 15-20 small ducts carry spermatozoa from the rete testis to the epididymis.

Blood-Testis Barrier: The blood-testis barrier is formed by Sertoli cells, which are connected by junctional complexes, including extensive tight junctions located towards the basal layer of the spermatogenic epithelium. (Option D) This barrier divides the seminiferous tubule into two compartments: the basal and the adluminal compartments. The adluminal compartment contains spermatids, isolating them from the systemic circulation.

The primary function of the blood-testis barrier is to protect developing gametes, which are antigenically different from somatic cells, from exposure to the immune system, thereby preventing an autoimmune response. Sertoli cells mediate all metabolic exchanges with the systemic compartment, ensuring the proper development of sperm.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the epithelial lining at the prostatic urethra?

explanation.text: The prostatic urethra is the portion of the male urethra that passes through the prostate gland. It is lined by transitional epithelium, also known as urothelium, which is continuous with the lining of the bladder.

Epithelial Lining of the Male Urethra Segment of Urethra Epithelial Lining Prostatic urethra Transitional epithelium (urothelium) Membranous urethra Stratified or pseudostratified columnar Penile (spongy) urethra Stratified columnar → non-keratinized squamous (distally) Fossa navicularis (tip) Non-keratinized stratified squamous Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (Option A): Incorrect because this is found at the external urethral meatus, not in the prostatic urethra.
**Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (Option B):** Incorrect as it lines the distal urethra (fossa navicularis), not the prostatic part.
**Stratified columnar epithelium (Option D):** Incorrect because it lines the membranous and proximal penile urethra, not the prostatic urethra.

questions.question: Which part of the nephron is characterized by cuboidal epithelial cells with a prominent brush border?

explanation.text: The PCT is characterized by cuboidal epithelial cells with a prominent brush border and is responsible for reabsorbing about 65-80% of the filtered solutes and water.

Part of Nephron Epithelial Lining Key Feature Main Function Renal Corpuscle Podocytes and simple squamous Contains glomerulus Blood filtration Proximal Convoluted Tubule Cuboidal with brush border Prominent brush border Major solute and water reabsorption Loop of Henle Simple squamous (descending) to cuboidal (ascending) U-shaped structure Urine concentration Distal Convoluted Tubule Cuboidal without brush border Basal striations Electrolyte balance Collecting Duct Cuboidal (principal and intercalated cells) Responsive to ADH Final urine concentration Option A: The renal corpuscle contains the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule, responsible for blood filtration.

It does not have cuboidal cells with a brush border. Option C: The loop of Henle has varying epithelial types (simple squamous to cuboidal) depending on the segment, but does not have a prominent brush border. Option D: The
DCT has cuboidal epithelial cells but lacks a brush border.

questions.question: Which of the following liver units is considered the most relevant functional unit for understanding patterns of toxic liver injury?

explanation.text: The parenchyma of liver is divided into 3 type of units: Classic Lobule: (Option A) Hexagonal shape with central vein and portal triads at corners Represents the basic structural unit of the liver Portal Lobule: (Option B) Triangular shape with portal triad at center and central veins at corners Emphasizes bile drainage Portal Acinus: Diamond-shaped unit between two portal triads Divided into three zones based on oxygen and nutrient supply: Zone 1 (periportal): Most oxygenated, more affected by toxins, least susceptible to ischaemia Zone 2 (midlobular): Intermediate oxygenation, Intermediate affected by toxins, Intermediate susceptible to ischaemia Zone 3 (centrilobular): Farthest from blood supply, least susceptible to toxicity, more susceptible to ischaemia Most relevant for understanding toxic liver injury due to its correlation with metabolic zonation Sinusoidal unit (Option D) is not a type of recognized liver unit.

questions.question: A 35-year-old patient with chronic hepatitis C undergoes a liver biopsy. The pathologist observes the classical hexagonal structure of liver lobules. Which of the following statements correctly regarding the blood flow and architecture within a liver lobule?

options.A: Blood flows from the central vein to the portal triad
options.B: The hepatic artery provides 70% of the liver's blood supply
options.C: Bile flows in the same direction as blood within the lobule
options.D: Sinusoids drain blood into the central vein

explanation.text: Blood flow in the liver is in the direction as given below: Hepatic artery/Portal vein → Hepatic Sinusoids → Central vein → Hepatic vein→ Inferior vena cava → Heart Liver architecture and hepatic sinusoids Liver blood supply Dual blood supply: Portal vein (70%) and hepatic artery (30%) O2 supply for Liver: Hepatic artery (60 % ) > Portal vein (40 % ) Portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood from the gut Hepatic artery provides oxygenated blood Liver lobule structure Hexagonal shape with central vein in the middle Portal triads at the corners, containing branches of: a) Portal vein b) Hepatic artery c) Bile duct Blood flow within the lobule Blood enters the lobule from branches of the portal vein and hepatic artery in the portal triad Flows through sinusoids between plates of hepatocytes Sinusoids drain into the central vein (centripetal flow) Central veins unite to form hepatic veins, which ultimately drain into the inferior vena cava Components of Hepatic sinusoids Endothelial cells: Form the discontinuous lining Kupffer cells: Resident macrophages attached to the endothelium Space of Disse: Perisinusoidal space between endothelium and hepatocytes Hepatic stellate cells (Ito cells): Located in the space of Disse, primary storage site of Vitamin A. Blood flows from the portal triad towards the central vein. (vs Option A) The portal vein provides about 70% of the blood supply (vs Option B), while the hepatic artery provides the remaining 30%. Bile flows in the opposite direction to blood (vs Option C), moving from hepatocytes towards the bile ducts in the portal triad.

questions.question: A 55-year-old patient presents with rectal bleeding. During the examination, the proctologist identifies a lesion at the junction between the columnar epithelium and the non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium in the anal canal. At which of the following anatomical landmarks is this lesion most likely located?

explanation.text: The lesion described is most likely located at the pectinate line (also known as the dentate line). This is the junction between the columnar epithelium of the upper anal canal and the non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium of the middle anal canal (pecten).

Region Length Epithelium Features Upper anal canal 15 mm Columnar epithelium 6-12 longitudinal folds called anal columns Between columns there are anal sinuses in which anal glands open Internal hemorrhoidal plexus in submucosa Pectinate (dentate) line - Transition zone Junction between columnar and non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium Formed by anal valves (lower ends of anal columns) Middle anal canal (Pecten) 15 mm Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium Bluish appearance due to dense venous plexus White line of Hilton (Option A) - Transition zone Lower limit of the pecten Junction between non-keratinized and keratinized epithelium Lower anal canal 8-10 mm Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (true skin) Contains hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands External hemorrhoidal plexus in submucosa Internal anal sphincter (Option C) - - Formed by smooth muscles present in muscularis externa External anal sphincter (Option D) - - Formed by skeletal muscles present in muscularis externa

The sample shows a mucosa without villi, numerous goblet cells, and an abundance of lymphoid tissue in the submucosa. The muscularis externa lacks taenia coli. Which part of the large intestine is this sample most likely from?

explanation.text: The biopsy sample with features of mucosa without villi, numerous goblet cells, absence of taenia coli and an abundance of lymphoid tissue in the submucosa is most likely from the appendix.

questions.question: Which of the following skin receptors is a rapidly adapting cell?

explanation.text: Pacinian corpuscle is a rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor that detects vibration and deep pressure. Skin Receptors Merkel cell - At basal layer for light touch sensation. Meissner's corpuscle - Two-point discrimination. Pacinian corpuscle - Carry pressure and vibration. Ruffini receptor - Dermal stretch. Free nerve endings - Conducts pain, crude touch and temperature.
**Rapidly adapting cells Slowly adapting cells Meissner corpuscle Pacinian corpuscle (Option D):** Merkel cell (Option A) Ruffini receptor (Option B) Free nerve endings (Option C)

questions.question: A pathologist is examining biopsy samples from different parts of the small intestine. Which of the following histological features would most likely indicate that the sample is from the ileum?

options.B: Abundant Brunner's glands in the submucosa
options.D: Thick circular folds in the lumen

explanation.text: Numerous large Peyer's patches are a characteristic feature of the ileum.

The table below discusses various histological features of small intestine: Feature Duodenum Jejunum Ileum Lumen and Wall Wider lumen, thicker wall Wider lumen, thicker wall Narrow lumen, thinner wall Circular Folds Large, thick circular folds Large, thick circular folds Small, few circular folds Villi Numerous broad villi with goblet cells Numerous tall villi with goblet cells Few, short and slender villi with goblet cells Brunner's Glands Present in submucosa Absent Absent Peyer's Patches Absent Very few, only in distal part Numerous, extending into mucosa Histology image Presence of numerous tall villi (Option A): This is more characteristic of the jejunum, not the ileum.
The ileum has fewer, shorter, and more slender villi.
**Brunner's glands (Option B):** are absent in both the jejunum and ileum.
**Large, thick circular folds (Option D):** are more prominent in the duodenum and jejunum. The ileum has smaller and fewer circular folds.

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient undergoes an endoscopic biopsy of the stomach due to persistent dyspepsia. Histological examination of the glandular tissue reveals cells that are columnar in shape, located in the lower half of the gland, and stain blue with hematoxylin. Which of the following statements is most likely true about these cells?

options.A: They secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor

explanation.text: The histological features describe chief cells of the gastric glands. Chief cell/peptic cell/ zymogen cells stain blue with hematoxylin due to basophilic cytoplasm, are columnar in shape and located in the basal (lower) part of the gastric pit.

Types of epithelium in stomach Region Epithelium Type Gastric Pits Characteristics Cardia Simple columnar Shallow Relatively thin mucosa Confined to small area near esophageal opening Fundus and Body Simple columnar Deep (occupying superficial one-fourth or less of the mucosa) Thicker mucosa Contains majority of gastric glands Pylorus Simple columnar Deep (occupying two-thirds of the depth of the mucosa) Thicker mucosa than cardia Contains specialized pyloric glands Gastric glands and their cells Cell Type Location Characteristics Function Chief cells (Peptic cells) Base of glands in fundus and body - Cuboidal or low columnar - Basophilic cytoplasm - Secretory granules in apical cytoplasm - Abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum Secrete pepsinogen (precursor of pepsin) Parietal cells (Oxyntic cells) Mostly in fundus and body - Large, ovoid or polyhedral - Eosinophilic cytoplasm - Narrow apical part reaching lumen - Intracellular canaliculi - Numerous mitochondria - Secrete hydrochloric acid - Produce intrinsic factor (Option A) Mucous neck cells Neck region of glands in fundus and body - Large cells with clear cytoplasm - Flattened nucleus pushed to base of cell Secrete mucus (Option B) G cells Mainly in pyloric glands - Endocrine cells - Contains secretory granules Secrete gastrin hormone (Option D) Endocrine cells (aka argentaffin cells) Scattered throughout gastric glands, more in pylorus - Near basal parts of gastric glands - Contain neurosecretory granules - Flattened, don't reach lumen - Secrete various hormones including gastrin - Some contain serotonin (5HT) Stem cells Isthmus of gastric glands Undifferentiated cells Replace other cell types, important for healing

questions.question: Which of the following statements with respect to histology of alveoli is INCORRECT?

options.A: The most abundant cell type lines form 70-90% of the alveolar surface and are of simple squamous type
options.B: Type II alveolar epithelial cells are microvilli containing cells which secrete surfactant similar to that of Clara cells
options.C: In some alveolar area, basement membrane of the endothelium fuses with that of the alveolar epithelium
options.D: Type I alveolar epithelial cells are involved in replacing the damaged type II alveolar cells

explanation.text: The statement is incorrect as type II alveolar epithelial cells are involved in replacing the damaged type I alveolar cells, not vice versa.

Histological features of alveoli: General histological features Alveolar Wall Very thin, lined by simple squamous epithelium Allows for efficient gas exchange Connective Tissue Contains collagen and elastic fibers Provides structural support Capillary Endothelium Extremely thin cells lining alveolar capillaries; Capillary basement membrane can fuse with alveolar basement membrane at certain places (Option C) Allows for efficient gas exchange Cells in Alveoli Type I Alveolar Epithelial Cells Simple squamous cells, cover 90% of alveolar surface (Option A) Main site of gas exchange Type II Alveolar Epithelial Cells Rounded secretory cells with microvilli Secrete pulmonary surfactant, can replace Type I cells (Option B) Type III Alveolar Cells (Brush Cells) Present in alveolar lining Function not fully understood Alveolar Macrophages (Dust Cells) Present in alveolar space Phagocytose particles, remove excess surfactant

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with chronic cough and shortness of breath. Bronchoscopy is performed, and a biopsy of the bronchial wall is taken. Histological examination reveals an epithelium with tall columnar cells bearing cilia on their apical surface, interspersed with goblet cells. Which part of the respiratory tract is most likely represented by this biopsy?

explanation.text: The epithelium described in the question- tall columnar cells with cilia and interspersed goblet cells- is characteristic of the trachea and principal bronchi.

Epithelium in Respiratory Tract Location Type of Epithelium Description Trachea and Main Bronchi Pseudostratified ciliated columnar Tall columnar cells with cilia, goblet cells present Bronchi and Bronchioles Simple ciliated columnar Single layer of ciliated columnar cells, fewer goblet cells Terminal Bronchioles (Option B) Simple ciliated columnar/cuboidal Single layer of cuboidal cells, some ciliated cells, no goblet cells, Clara cells Respiratory Bronchioles (Option C) Simple ciliated cuboidal to simple squamous Single layer of ciliated cuboidal cells or single layer of simple squamous, no goblet cells, Clara cells Alveoli (Option D) Simple squamous Thin, flat cells for efficient gas exchange

questions.question: Which histological feature most accurately describes the epithelium responsible for mucociliary clearance in the upper respiratory tract?

options.B: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells
options.C: Simple cuboidal epithelium with Clara cells
options.D: Simple squamous epithelium with alveolar macrophages

explanation.text: The epithelium responsible for mucociliary clearance in the upper respiratory tract is the respiratory epithelium. Respiratory epithelium The respiratory epithelium is predominantly composed of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with numerous goblet cells in the trachea and larger bronchi, which is essential for mucociliary clearance.

This type of epithelium has the appearance of multiple layers due to the varying positions of nuclei, but all cells are in contact with the basement membrane, making it pseudostratified. Goblet cells: These cells are responsible for producing mucus, which traps particles, a critical component of the mucociliary clearance system.

Cilia: Ciliated cells beat in a coordinated manner to propel mucus and trapped particles toward the pharynx, preventing the accumulation of foreign materials in the lower airways. The epithelial lining changes along the respiratory tract, becoming simpler (cuboidal or squamous) in the smaller airways and alveoli to facilitate gas exchange.

**Stratified squamous epithelium, non-keratinized (Option A):** Found in areas subjected to mechanical stress, like the oropharynx, but lacks the cilia and goblet cells needed for mucociliary clearance.

**Simple cuboidal epithelium with Clara cells (Option C):** Found in terminal bronchioles, where Clara cells secrete surfactant-like substances, but this epithelium is not responsible for the primary mucociliary clearance in the larger airways.

**Simple squamous epithelium with alveolar macrophages (Option D):** Found in the alveoli, this epithelium is thin to facilitate gas exchange, while alveolar macrophages perform phagocytosis of debris. It does not participate in mucociliary clearance.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man presents with difficulty swallowing and a mild hoarse voice. Examination reveals no significant findings, and imaging shows no abnormal masses in the oropharynx. A biopsy is taken from a structure in the oropharynx that histologically shows a mixture of stratified squamous epithelium and pseudostratified columnar epithelium. This structure also contains seromucous glands and an elastic cartilage core. Which of the following structures is most likely biopsied?

explanation.text: The structure biopsied in this scenario is the epiglottis. Histology of the Epiglottis: The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped structure that serves as a flap during swallowing, closing the laryngeal inlet to prevent food from entering the airway.

Its upper surface is covered by stratified squamous epithelium (in the area exposed to mechanical wear from food), while the lower surface (facing the airway) has pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium (respiratory epithelium). The core of the epiglottis contains elastic cartilage, which provides flexibility and support. There are seromucous glands present, especially in the lamina propria, which help keep the surface moist.

Epiglottis Histology of the Palate: The hard palate is lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on its oral side, with a bony core. It lacks elastic cartilage and respiratory epithelium. (Option A) The soft palate has a surface of non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on the oral side, and pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium on the nasal side.

Unlike the epiglottis, the core of the soft palate consists of skeletal muscle rather than cartilage. (Option B) Palate Vocal cords (Option D): The true vocal cords are lined by stratified squamous epithelium, but they lack pseudostratified columnar epithelium and elastic cartilage. Instead, they have a ligamentous core (vocal ligament) and skeletal muscle (vocalis muscle).
